slides.page_title: Map Internals: Buckets, Growth, Swiss Tables

items: Groups of 8 slots plus a SIMD-scannable control word
The control word holds 7-bit hash fragments, scanned in one shot
Measurably faster lookups and less memory on large maps
Internal layout changed; language semantics did not

blocks.title: Randomly seeded hashing
blocks.text: The per-process seed defeats hash-flooding denial of service — and is the direct cause of unordered iteration.

items: A map that held 1M entries keeps that memory at `len(m) == 0`
Delete never gives bucket count back
Build a fresh map and drop the old one to reclaim
Above a size threshold, keys or values are stored as pointers to heap
So choose `map[K]*BigStruct` deliberately, not by accident
Growth relocates entries, so `&m[k]` cannot exist
That relocation IS the reason for the non-addressability rule
The runtime picks a random start bucket AND a random offset inside it
Two ranges over the SAME unmodified map can differ
It stops code depending on an order the runtime may change

blocks.title: `fmt` lies to you
blocks.text: `fmt` prints maps in sorted key order, which convinces people iteration is ordered. It is not — that sort is only for printing.

items: Never assert map range order in a test
It passes locally and fails in CI — the seed differs
`maps.Keys`/`maps.Values` (Go 1.23+) return iterators
Materialize with `slices.Collect` or `slices.Sorted`

slides.page_title: Map Iteration Order & Deleting During Range

items: Deleting the current key is the standard filter idiom
A new entry may or may not be visited in the same loop
To add, build a second map or collect keys first

blocks.q: Two goroutines write the same map — what happens?
a_bullets: `fatal error: concurrent map writes` — the process dies
It is not a panic; `recover` cannot save you
The detector is best-effort, not a guarantee
Use `-race` to catch it reliably in tests

blocks.title: When sync.Map fits
items: Append-only caches, written once, read many
Disjoint key sets per goroutine
Otherwise a plain map behind `RWMutex` wins

blocks.title: Small n flips the answer
blocks.text: Under roughly 8-16 elements, a linear scan of a slice often BEATS a map — cache locality plus the hashing cost you skipped.

items: Slices allow duplicates; maps collapse them by key
Fastest dedupe: `map[T]struct{}` plus an output slice for order
Slices give stable order for free; maps need an explicit sort

slides.page_title: Slice vs Map: Choosing and Trading Off

items: `encoding/json` emits Go map keys sorted, so JSON output is stable
The nil asymmetry is worth memorising: nil slice usable, nil map read-only
The map holds positions into the slice
Delete is the hard part — every later index shifts
So encapsulate both, never expose them raw

blocks.title: Deciding in one line
blocks.text: Order or small n: slice. Keyed lookup at scale: map. Both: keep both, wrapped in a type that owns the invariant.

items: Ignoring append's return value — the mutation goes nowhere; `go vet` catches it
`make([]T,n)` when you meant `make([]T,0,n)` — n zeros, then your data
Forgetting `s[i:j:j]` when handing a slice to code that appends
Returning a sub-slice of a buffer you will reuse
Holding a small slice of a huge read and pinning the whole array
Not nil-ing removed pointer elements when the slice outlives the removal

blocks.title: Not optional
blocks.text: If the slice outlives the delete, the tail slot still references the object. Nil it, or the leak is permanent.

items: Assuming range order is stable, especially in golden-file tests
Concurrent writes with no lock — a fatal crash, not a recoverable one
Lazy map construction at the call site instead of in the constructor

spec.label: a slice is a WINDOW onto an array

blocks.title: One sentence
blocks.text: append either writes through the window or silently cuts a new one — and capacity alone decides which.

blocks.title: Run before merge
items: `go vet` for discarded appends
tests with `-race`
presize with `make(..., 0, n)` where n is known
clone at every API boundary that stores or returns a slice
sort keys wherever map output is user-visible

caption.text: Part 2 of GO SLICES & MAPS: THE FIELD MANUAL. A Go slice is a 24-byte window onto an array you cannot see — and append either writes through that window or silently cuts a new one, depending on capacity nobody at the call site knows about. 10 pages on backing arrays, three-index slicing, the 1.18 growth rule, Swiss-table maps in 1.24, why range order is randomized on purpose, and the aliasing bugs that only show up in production. Save it for the next code review where somebody returns `sc.Bytes()`.
